newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH FINMIN AGAINST PEASANTS' FARM PROPOSALS.
newsitem.headline: POLISH FINMIN AGAINST PEASANTS' FARM PROPOSALS.

text.p: The Polish finance ministry on Thursday criticised the co-ruling Peasant Party's demand to offer advance payments to farmers for the grain harvest, saying it could hit the budget and destabilise the food market.

Finance Minister Marek Belka said the proposal, which the Peasants said must be approved within a week or they will press for the prime minister's dismissal, could cost the national budget up to 260 million zlotys, more than it could bear.

"This proposal could prove very costly if there is little demand for grains...and it could destabilise the grain market," Belka said, adding it could aggravate the already difficult situation on the farm market after July's catastrophic floods.
Belka said the ministry had drafted an alternative and much cheaper plan to help farmers before the harvest, which had been approved by Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz.
Under the plan, farmers would get special storage certificates for grains they would put in earmarked storehouses.
The farmers would be entitled to seek budget-subsidised loans in banks and present the certificates as collateral.

They would pay back the loans after they sell the stored grains. If they do not find any buyers by the end of the year, the stored grain would be bought by the Agriculture Market Agency (ARR), the food market regulator, for a minimum price.

Under a controversial proposal by the Peasant Party's Agriculture Minister Jaroslaw Kalinowski, farmers would get cheap loans from the ARR for grains they could keep at home, then sell on the market for a commercial price or to the agency if this proved impossible. @
Cimoszewicz refused to discuss Kalinowski's scheme at a cabinet meeting earlier this week, prompting a quarrel between the Peasants and the prime minister's ex-communist party.
The Peasants said they would seek to remove Cimoszewicz from his post unless the cabinet approved their proposals by August 12.
Many analysts and politicians have said the ultimatum is part of the Peasants' campaign for general elections due on September 21 and was aimed at ensuring the support of the rural electorate.
